content.title: About
content.content: Alfredo sauce with added vegetables is a creamy sauce made from cream, Parmesan cheese, and butter, enriched with diced carrots, broccoli, zucchini, and sweet bell pepper. It combines the smooth, buttery flavor of classic Alfredo with a subtle sweetness and crunch from the vegetables, making it a versatile topping for pasta, rice, and casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Alfredo sauce was created in the early 1920s at the restaurant "Alfredo" in Rome.
Adding vegetables boosts fiber and vitamin content without altering the signature creamy taste.
Vegetables are usually steamed before being mixed in to preserve color and nutrients.
In American cuisine, Alfredo sauce often serves as a base for dishes like chicken and broccoli pasta.
The combination of Parmesan and vegetables creates a more complex aromatic profile than the classic sauce alone.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vegetables such as broccoli and bell pepper provide B6 and folate, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The added vegetables increase the fiber content, aiding normal digestion.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Parmesan cheese supplies calcium, and the cream is often fortified with vitamin D, both beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli and carrots contain beta‑carotene and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin A from carrots and vitamin C from bell pepper contribute to a stronger immune system.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream and cheese contain lactose; those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Being cream‑based, the sauce is high in fat and calories, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Parmesan adds salt; individuals monitoring sodium should opt for a reduced‑salt version.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Alfredo sauce with vegetables pairs well with pasta (spaghetti, fettuccine), rice, couscous, and works as a base for casseroles and vegetable lasagnas. Heat gently over medium heat, adding a splash of water or broth to reach the desired consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 5 days after opening. It can be frozen for up to 2 months in an airtight container. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Peking duck is a large domesticated bird originally bred in China. It is prized for its tender, juicy meat, aromatic skin, and ability to gain weight quickly, making it a popular choice for roasting, braising, and stir‑fry dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peking duck is the star of the classic Chinese dish “Peking Duck,” where the skin is served crisp and the meat remains succulent.
The breed was introduced to Europe in the 17th century and has become one of the most common commercial duck varieties.
Peking ducks grow fast; by 12‑14 weeks they reach a market weight of about 3–4 kg.
The skin contains more fat than most chicken breeds, giving dishes a distinctive richness.
In Chinese culture the duck symbolizes prosperity and is often served at festive occasions.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Duck meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support hemoglobin formation and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peking duck is abundant in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fats
items.content: The fat in duck includes omega‑6 and modest amounts of omega‑3, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: Selenium from duck meat contributes to the body’s antioxidant defenses.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Duck is richer in fat than chicken, so people watching calorie intake should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked duck may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Bird allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry meat.

items.title: Cholesterol level
items.content: Duck contains higher cholesterol than most white meats, which should be considered in heart‑related conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peking duck can be roasted, braised, grilled, or steamed. The classic preparation involves roasting until the skin is crisp, then serving the meat with thin pancakes, hoisin sauce, and fresh vegetables. Duck meat also works well in soups, salads, and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh duck should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen duck in the fridge before cooking.

lobster-with-sauce-puerto-rican-style.title: Lobster with sauce, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Lobster is a prized seafood with tender meat, popular throughout the Caribbean. In the Puerto Rican style it is served with a fragrant sauce made from tomatoes, sweet peppers, garlic, olive oil, and spices such as cumin, oregano, and paprika. The dish balances the natural sweetness of the lobster with the bright, slightly spicy notes of the sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lobster is considered a delicacy and is often served at celebrations and festivals in Puerto Rico.
The traditional sauce is prepared with local tomatoes, sweet peppers (pimiento) and aromatic herbs, giving it a distinctive Caribbean flavor.
Puerto Rican lobsters are typically caught in the Atlantic coastal waters where the temperature hovers around 24 °C, producing sweet, firm meat.
The dish is commonly accompanied by rice, beans, and fried plantains as side dishes.
In 1642 the first major seafood market opened in Puerto Rico, and lobster quickly became one of its main export items.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Lobster meat provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other seafoods, lobster contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in zinc and selenium
items.content: These minerals support immune function and act as antioxidants.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lobster supplies vitamin B12, B6 and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3s help maintain cardiovascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to lobster, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Lobster contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: In certain regions lobsters can accumulate cadmium or mercury; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Cooking lobster too long makes the meat tough and dry and can diminish its nutritional value.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lobster is usually boiled or steamed until the shell turns bright red and the meat is pink. It is then drizzled with hot sauce and served with rice, beans, fried plantains, or a fresh salad. The meat can be pulled from the claws and tail and eaten with hands or a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh lobster should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days, tightly wrapped. Frozen lobster retains quality for up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen lobster in the fridge before cooking and prepare promptly.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, cooked with milk is a ready‑to‑eat product obtained by boiling rice in milk. It has a soft, creamy texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and is often used in baby foods, desserts, and as a quick breakfast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice with milk is a traditional dish in many Asian countries, especially Japan (okān) and India (kheer).
The combination improves the bioavailability of some B‑vitamins.
In Soviet cuisine, rice with milk was commonly served as a sweet porridge with sugar or honey.
When prepared correctly, the product retains most nutrients from both ingredients.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice carbohydrates are quickly digested, providing rapid energy.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk supplies calcium essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D in milk aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The smooth, creamy texture is easy on the stomach, especially for children and sensitive adults.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Combining plant protein from rice with milk protein offers a complete amino‑acid profile.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice has a high GI, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: If sweetened, the product can raise blood sugar levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy rice with milk hot as a breakfast, add fruit, nuts, or honey. It can be used in desserts, casseroles, and as a base for baby meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Check smell and texture before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is a lean meat from deer, high in protein and low in fat. In this dish it is served with boiled or roasted potatoes and seasonal vegetables such as carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens, accompanied by a savory gravy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered a more diet‑friendly red meat because of its low fat content.
In the wild, deer obtain most of their nutrients from grasses and leaves, giving the meat a higher proportion of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Traditionally, venison has been a staple in northern Europe and Asia where deer were a key food source.
Potatoes, carrots and broccoli are commonly paired with venison because they retain their nutrients when roasted.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables like spinach or kale add iron and vitamin K to the meal.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Venison provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with other red meats, venison contains less saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: The meat is rich in heme iron and zinc, which aid immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Venison supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegetables add fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli, carrots and leafy greens provide vitamins A, C, K and dietary fiber, supporting digestion and immunity.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Wild venison may harbor parasites; it should be cooked thoroughly to a safe internal temperature.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Venison is rich in purines, which can be problematic for individuals with gout.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to venison.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies can be salty; adjust added salt according to dietary needs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison can be roasted, pan‑seared, or braised, served with boiled or roasted potatoes and vegetables. Gravy is made from stock, cream and spices, poured over the meat and sides. Vegetables are best lightly sautéed or steamed to retain crunch and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh venison should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. Frozen meat retains quality for 6‑12 months at –18 °C. Store vegetables in a sealed container in the fridge, and keep any leftovers refrigerated for up to 3 days.
